Summary with SLOOS overlay

- Policy stance: The FOMC held the target range at 5.25–5.50% and will continue QT, seeking “greater confidence” that inflation is moving sustainably to 2% before cutting. Language that risks are moving into “better balance” is a mild dovish shift, but the Committee remains data‑dependent and vigilant.

- SLOOS signals on credit conditions: The July 2024 Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey indicates private credit remains a headwind.
  - Business credit: Banks, on net, kept C&I lending standards tight (in many cases unchanged at already‑tight levels) and reported subdued loan demand from both large and middle‑market firms. Reasons cited include a weaker/uncertain economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, and industry‑specific concerns. Spreads and covenants remained relatively restrictive.
  - CRE: Standards stayed tight and demand remained weak, with elevated concern around office valuations and refinance risk. Collateral valuations and vacancy trends continue to weigh on approvals.
  - Residential real estate: Banks reported tight standards for most mortgage categories, with demand still soft; HELOCs saw cautious underwriting.
  - Consumer credit: For credit cards and autos, banks continued to tighten terms—higher spreads, lower credit limits, and more stringent underwriting. Many banks reported higher minimum required credit scores and tighter policies for borrowers near score cutoffs, and some lifted minimum payment requirements on revolving accounts. Demand was generally weaker, while delinquencies have been drifting up from low levels.
  - Bank funding/liquidity: Conditions have stabilized versus 2023, which reduces acute stress, but lenders remain conservative.

- Implications: The SLOOS’s persistently restrictive credit supply and weak loan demand temper the FOMC’s “solid” growth tone and the mild dovish nuance from “better balance.” These data point to continued headwinds for capex, CRE refinancing, and consumer durables, reinforcing disinflation but adding downside risk to activity. This supports a patient stance (no urgency to hike) while awaiting clearer evidence on inflation; it also argues against a decisively positive read of the outlook.

Net read: Cautiously guarded. The SLOOS tightness nudges the assessment modestly more cautious than an FSR‑only lens.
